front: Why does Hudson say judging someone hurts you physically?
back: To judge, you have to clench and constrict your muscles.
extra: He compares the small payoff, feeling better than them, to an addiction.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

front: When someone judges you, what does Hudson say they are doing to themselves?
back: Judging themselves about ten times harder.
extra: The more judgmental a person is, the less good they feel about themselves. So the first person to stop judging is you.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

text: Hudson calls judgment an emotional {{c1::eddy}}: the same feeling circles in place, so joy cannot show up.
extra: A backwater with no flow. Guilt and shame make the same kind of eddy, he says in another interview.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

front: Does keeping a judgment silent hide it from the other person, in Hudson's view?
back: No. Your face and body language show it, and people know.
extra: So judging says, in effect: do not date me, buy from me or work with me.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

front: Why does Hudson warn against telling yourself "I shouldn't judge"?
back: That "should" is one more judgment, now aimed at you.
extra: Instead, notice the pain of judging and what life you want, and let yourself move that way.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

front: What feeling does Hudson warn will come in once you stop judging?
back: Love, which can be the scariest feeling, because it opens you to heartbreak.
extra: He says heartbreak only increases your capacity to love. Go slowly and take care of yourself.
source_title: How To Stop Being Judgmental - 3 Ways

front: How does Hudson tell a choice from a decision?
back: A choice happens all day with no effort. A decision starts when fear says something could go wrong.
extra: So if you are deciding, you are already afraid and trying to avoid something.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: In a hard decision, what does Hudson say you are really trying to avoid?
back: An emotion, not an outcome.
extra: If you knew being homeless would make you happier than ever, it would scare you much less.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: Why does living by principles stop needing discipline, in Hudson's account?
back: You keep seeing that it works when you follow them and fails when you do not.
extra: Discipline is needed only at first. Then hard decisions turn back into easy choices.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: What does Hudson's principle "embrace intensity" mean?
back: Do not create intensity, but feel into any discomfort that shows up.
extra: He keeps it because he decides clearly when he avoids nothing.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: His story: over time, which intensity did embracing fear, anger and failure teach him to allow?
back: Excitement, joy and pleasure, which he says are far more intense.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: What does Hudson say about the principles you live by now?
back: You already have some, chosen without thought: stay out of trouble, please people, get angry when you do not get your way.
extra: Just seeing them starts to change things. Then run experiments to find what works.
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: What does Hudson call the most efficient way to change your consciousness?
back: Change your behaviour: do something different 10 times and see what happens.
extra: Example: where his old principle said "get angry", the new one says "ask a how or what question".
source_title: Every decision you struggle with has one thing in common

front: How do you play Hudson's happy money game?
back: Two people take turns proposing how to work together, payment included.
extra: He has played it for over a decade.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

text: In the happy money game, the winner proposes a deal that both people are {{c1::excited about}}, not just happy with or able to live with.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: His story: what did the game produce with his first famous client, who liked to win but skipped the inner work?
back: A high fee that doubled, then tripled, if the client failed to do the work.
extra: Losing money when he skipped the work helped him understand himself.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: His story: why was his second wealthy client not allowed to pay him?
back: Everyone wanted him for his money. Free help was the only way he could believe it was not bought.
extra: Both clients later repaid him many times over in referrals and support.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What rule does Hudson live by about work for money?
back: He will not do anything for money that he would not do for free.
extra: He also never coaches anyone for pay before coaching them once for free, so both can see if it fits.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What does the effort to put a deal together predict, in Hudson's experience?
back: The effort it will take to keep the deal going.
extra: From his venture capital years: a deal that was hard to make was high-maintenance later.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

text: Hudson's tennis image: aim at the {{c1::basket}} (money) and you hit it now and then. Aim at a {{c2::quarter}} inside it (your mission) and you hit the basket far more often.
extra: A coach put a quarter where the basket had been. The player never hit the quarter but would have hit the basket every time. He tells it in the Ali Abdaal interview too.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What two relationships to money does Hudson contrast?
back: A consumer's: money is using you. An investor's: you use money as a tool to build the life you want.
extra: You already use money as a tool all day, for a bed, for games, for freedom.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: When money keeps going badly for you, what does Hudson say to look for?
back: The frame you hold about it, such as "there is not enough" or "if I get it, you don't".
extra: Money and deals are usually framed as zero-sum. He notes there is more money now than 10 years ago.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: Why does Hudson call money non-linear?
back: Value you give freely can bring far more back later, so insisting on a fair price up front can push people away.
extra: His example: one deal led to 10 more wealthy clients. A job applicant who sends sample work beats one who names a price.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What does the happy money game need before you can play it?
back: Consent and trust: two people who both want neither to lose.
extra: It works for any agreement, even who does the dishes.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: Where does Hudson say the happy money game may not fit?
back: A salary negotiation with a boss, where everyone expects to negotiate and there are few variables.
extra: It fits where haggling would destroy trust, as with a coaching client.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What useful habit does the game force, even if you play it alone?
back: Thinking through what could go wrong, not just how great the deal will be.
extra: Ask yourself what you need to be happy with this over the next two or three years.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: Why does Hudson say to celebrate when someone wins the game?
back: It keeps the competitive spirit, aimed at finding the best deal rather than getting the most.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: What is the biggest lesson of the happy money game, in Hudson's view?
back: There is always a solution where both of you win.
extra: Fear makes thinking binary: me or you, plus or minus. That holds in a fight with a partner or a boss too.
source_title: The Game that Changed my Relationship with Money

front: In "connection over perfection", why does Hudson say perfection fails?
back: It cannot be reached and is not even defined; the mind always finds a better way.
extra: We learned it as children to avoid criticism. No one has driven or talked perfectly.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: In "connection over perfection", what does connection become?
back: The yardstick: how connected you feel with yourself and others while you do the thing.
extra: A product made to connect with customers beats a perfect product, he says.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Try now, 1 minute: pick what you are doing, even riding a bike. Ask how you could do it with a deeper sense of connection with yourself.
back: Notice what changes in how it feels, and in how well it goes.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: In "enjoyment over management", what are dirty and clean fuel?
back: Dirty fuel is "I am not enough". Clean fuel is enjoyment.
extra: He said this to a 45-year-old with a $30 million house who was miserable.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: How does Hudson use a car to explain "enjoyment is efficiency"?
back: Ending the day exhausted means you burned a lot of energy. Ending it glad, with energy left, means you ran efficiently.
extra: That is what enjoying yourself looks like.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Why does managing people work worse than enjoying them, in Hudson's view?
back: People resist being managed or manipulated, but they want to be with someone who enjoys them.
extra: He also points out that people who manipulate to get their way are rarely happy.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: What are the two meanings of enjoyment in "enjoyment over management"?
back: Doing what you enjoy, and learning to enjoy what you are doing.
extra: If you enjoy the process, you end up where you want to be, not where you thought you wanted to be.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: What does Hudson take from the book Descartes' Error?
back: Decisions are made in the brain's emotional centre. Without it, IQ stays the same but tiny choices take ages.
extra: His reading: we use logic only to predict how we will feel. The book is by the neuroscientist Antonio Damasio; Hudson's summary was not checked.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: His story: what did Hudson find on a list of everything he disliked about himself, months after writing it?
back: What had changed came on its own. Nothing he had told himself he "should" change had changed.
extra: He wrote it in a bare room in Mill Valley and forgot about it for six to eight months.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Why does Hudson say a "should" fails to start change?
back: A should is a form of shame, and shame exists to stop things, not to start them.
extra: Example: a child shamed for farting learns to hold it in. Stagnation follows.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: What does Hudson mean, and not mean, by "want"?
back: The natural pull to your next step, like a branch growing toward light. Not craving or neediness.
extra: Children aged 0 to 7 follow their wants and develop faster than at any other age.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Besides fear of not getting it, why does wanting feel scary, per Hudson?
back: Getting what you want will redefine you; you become a different person.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: His story: what was his chase for enlightenment in his twenties, looking back?
back: His perfectionism in another form; he hoped to never have a problem again.
extra: Teachers told him he was already there. The tension left only when he understood his own nature, not from a perfect routine.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: In "empowerment over power", why does power make you afraid?
back: Power rests on other people agreeing that you have it, so it can be taken away.
extra: By a gun, a loss of money, or an audience that stops liking you.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: In "empowerment over power", what is empowerment?
back: Knowing deeply who you are, so you have nothing to defend and cannot have it taken away.
extra: His example: Nelson Mandela in prison.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Try next time someone does something that embarrasses you: instead of making them stop, ask what you need to be fully yourself now, a person you respect.
back: Notice that the question needs nothing from the other person.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: In "love over defense", what does each act of defending yourself show, per Hudson?
back: That you think something is wrong with you, a part of you that you will not accept.
extra: If you say the sky is blue and someone says purple, you do not defend. Call you a liar and you might.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: His story: what happened after a friend called him an asshole and told him to stop defending it?
back: He accepted and loved that part, and over three months he acted that way less.
extra: At Bodega Bay. What we resist persists; loving it changes it.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Does an open heart mean you will be taken advantage of, per Hudson?
back: No. That fear mixes love with wanting to be liked. Love can say "I love you" and still refuse your deal.
extra: His examples are Gandhi, Martin Luther King and any great mother.
source_title: After 14 Years of Coaching, This Is What I See Hold Most People Back

front: Why does reaching a goal feel good for a moment, in Hudson's view?
back: Not because of the goal, but because for a moment there is nothing to want.
extra: Then a new goal comes. Chasing goals brings pressure, like game point in tennis.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What does Hudson say purpose is, besides a career?
back: How you do things as much as what you do.
extra: He says he could find his purpose working at the post office. Searching for it assumes you were not born with it.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: His story: what did he find when a peer's billion-dollar win hit him like a kick in the stomach?
back: The feeling first came when he tried to win his father's love. Money had taken his father's place.
extra: He says money is often a projection of something you needed as a child.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: His story: what changed when he saw that billionaires felt the same lack he did?
back: He saw money could never satisfy him, and from then it came to him easily.
extra: He calls money a carrot on a stick, and says fulfillment brings money rather than the reverse.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: How does Hudson show that money is not scarce?
back: Look out any window: the glass, the road sign, the steel. Someone made money from each.
extra: Only the thinking is constricted, he says. Making money can be an expression of who you are.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: His story: what did his daughter's 50-rejection challenge get her, and what does it show?
back: A summer job in Panama. Willingness to face rejection matters more than which college she attends.
extra: When the paperwork stalled, she asked people in suits outside a Sacramento government building until one helped.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What does Hudson say overwhelm is?
back: A stuck emotion: one too intense to feel, so you push it down and compartmentalize it.
extra: To clear it, slow down enough to take it in, or express it, which he says is faster. Express it alone, never at a person, and stop if you feel flooded.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: How does Hudson describe the end point of emotional fluidity?
back: You love having every emotion. They move through you with ease, and they do not control you.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

text: Hudson: on the back side of helplessness is {{c1::empowerment}}; of sadness, {{c2::relief}}; of anger, {{c3::clarity}}.
extra: This is why he says you can learn to enjoy even hard feelings.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hudson's tube image, what is anger when it is not twisted?
back: A clear boundary held with love.
extra: Twisted one way it becomes "I'm not angry", the other way rage. We only get angry about what we care about.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

text: Hudson's image: joy is the {{c1::matriarch}} of the family of emotions. She will not come into a house unless all her children are welcome.
extra: So holding down anger leaves no room for joy.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: When a feeling comes and the mind says "if I'm sad I'll be sad forever", what does Hudson suggest you say?
back: Tell the mind you have heeded it for years, and will now give the feeling about 20 minutes.
extra: Then let yourself feel what is happening.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Try it with care: how does Hudson suggest someone face painful criticism, such as bad reviews?
back: Read them while a loved one holds you, without reassuring you. Keep breathing; watch for a tight jaw or throat.
extra: Go only to the point where it feels like enough, then come back later. Do not push your nervous system out of regulation.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Why does Hudson say trying to fix someone's feelings backfires?
back: It tells them they are wrong to feel it.
extra: Instead, just be with them in loving attention. He says men in the West feel a strong urge to fix.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: If your partner doubts their own good work, how often should you reassure them, per Hudson?
back: Say your view once. Chasing them into feeling better is about your own discomfort.
extra: A story he tells: a depressed Quaker said the friend who washed his feet each week helped most, by treating him as whole.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What does Hudson say about the roles two people hold, such as worrier and optimist?
back: One person holds each side. Drop your role, and the other can drop theirs.
extra: Once, when an employee called their own work bad and he agreed, they started defending it.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: When your partner is upset with you, what does Hudson suggest instead of defending?
back: Say you want to hear all about it and ask what they want, without promising to agree.
extra: In most fights both people feel they are only defending, and both feel attacked by the other's defense.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What does Hudson say we only get triggered by?
back: What we secretly think is true about ourselves.
extra: So taking an attack, even from an internet troll, with an open heart wears down the ego.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: When a parent is hurt by your career choice, what kind of "I'm sorry" does Hudson suggest?
back: "I'm sorry my choices are hurting you": sorry they hurt, without taking blame or giving up your choice.
extra: If they say you would stop if you were sorry, he would answer that he wants them not to hurt but will not act against himself.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

text: Hudson: as people grow, the sense of self widens from {{c1::me}} to family, tribe, nation, humanity and the ecosystem, until it becomes {{c2::universal}} again.
extra: A small child cannot tell their wishes from the world's. The universal sense of self feels like a memory; he says this is what people call awakening.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

text: Hudson: the sense of time widens from a child's few days, to the average American's {{c1::three and a half years}}, to {{c2::seven generations}}, until infinity becomes the depth of a moment.
extra: The seven-generation example is from Native American thinking.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Why does Hudson avoid the word "enlightenment"?
back: It suggests being finished, and he has never seen growth end.
extra: After his own awakening his first thought was "this never ends". He says people who think they are done get stuck in that identity.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: How can inner peace become a way to avoid feeling, per Hudson?
back: People escape into the peace and skip their emotions. He asks them: where is the joy?
extra: Getting back into the emotions can feel like hell at first. Then the joy comes.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: His story: what answered the question "what am I essentially?" that came to him 10 times a day?
back: Nothing did. The question itself was the brilliance, not any answer.
extra: He chased awakening for about ten years. He says the effort slowed it, as chasing pushes things away.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Why is "be undefended" a strange instruction, per Hudson?
back: It is an undoing, not a doing. If you try hard to be undefended, you are defended.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Why does Hudson call his work applied self-discovery, not spiritual teaching?
back: Tools must be used in the world, where you can see if they work. Meditating alone, he fooled himself for years.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Why does Hudson prefer listening to yourself over following morality?
back: Morality turns being good into an obligation, which takes the joy out. Being good to people is joyful anyway.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: Try now, 2 minutes: list a few ways you changed in the last five years. How many of them needed a "should"?
back: Notice that, in Hudson's view, real change rarely came from a should.
extra: Then the reverse: the habit you have told yourself to change for years is still there.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: When a parent asks how to motivate a teen, what does Hudson ask back?
back: What are you trying not to feel?
extra: Telling a child to be different says they are broken, and no one wants to listen to someone who sees them as broken.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hand in Hand Parenting (Patty Wipfler), what is a listening partnership?
back: A place for the parent to let out feelings about raising kids, where it cannot hurt the kids.
extra: Hudson raised his children with this method, for about ages 0 to 8. Her book is "Listen".
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hand in Hand Parenting (Patty Wipfler), what is staylistening?
back: Letting a child's emotions be big while you stay with them in loving attention.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hand in Hand Parenting (Patty Wipfler), what is playlistening?
back: Rough-and-tumble play with a child so that fear can move.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hand in Hand Parenting (Patty Wipfler), what kind of limits does a parent set?
back: Gentle but firm: stay close and insist, as the adult.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: In Hand in Hand Parenting (Patty Wipfler), what is special time?
back: Time where you join the child's world fully, rather than pulling them into yours.
extra: Hudson calls it going down the rabbit hole: if it is a tea party, have tea.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: His story: how did Hudson test Hand in Hand Parenting, which his wife chose?
back: As a clean experiment: do whatever she said for three months without resisting, then judge.
extra: He calls the result remarkable, and says it was a big practice in feeling his own emotions.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What does Hudson watch for when giving his children money?
back: That money is not used so they, or he, can avoid a feeling.
extra: After school he will fund their growth, not throw money at a problem.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment

front: What advice does Hudson give someone turning 30?
back: Enjoy the softening: around 30 the sense of knowing everything flips, with less to prove.
extra: He adds that for many men the prime is around 40.
source_title: Joe Hudson: How your Emotions Drive your Success & Fulfillment
